items.title: Erykah Badu Takes Us on a Cosmic Trip For ‘Breezy’ Late-Night Performance: Watch
items.summary:
With Erykah Badu behind the wheel, what could possibly go wrong?

The five-time Grammy Award winning R&B star stopped by NBC’s The Tonight Show on Tuesday night (Nov. 24), for a performance of “Breezy,” lifted from her collaborative album with The Alchemist , Before the World Blows: The Abi and Alan Experiment .

For the musical spot, Badu drives night owls to a place they’ve never been. With a steering wheel in her hands, Badu embarks on a cosmic journey, a psychedelic trip. Once arrived at her destination, she pulls back and gets to work with her full band as “Breezy” blends into Elton John’s “Bennie and the Jets.”

Before the World Blows: The Abi and Alan Experiment is a 16-track journey into the minds of two important artists in their respective fields that came together to forge a work of art. The catalyst? More than three years ago, Badu told her longtime creative partner Cold Cris that she had always wanted to rap over Mobb Deep’s “The Realest,” a gritty Alchemist production.

Then, reps say, The Alchemist sent Badu a collection of instrumental beats, which she deconstructed and molded into tracks, before testing their creations with live audiences in 2024 and 2025, performing in intimate, phone-free spaces.

The co-produced collection dropped in August, the result of 18 months’ recording in Dallas and Los Angeles, and features contributions from DJ Creole Princess, Westside Gunn , Joi, DRAM , Steve Lacy , Thundercat , Earl Sweatshirt , Kamasi Washington , DJ Quik on percussion and Young Guru contributing to the project’s mixing efforts.

Before the World Blows: The…

items.title: Amanda Seyfried had to get a five-factor security app just to read ‘You Can See Everything’ script
items.summary:
Amanda Seyfried has spoken about her secretive appearance in record-breaking documentary You Can See Everything .

READ MORE: ‘You Can See Everything’ review: a three-hour odyssey of deception, doubt and dodgy dealings 

Directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, You Can See Everything captures Elizabeth Holmes’ final few weeks at home before the health businesswoman went to jail following her conviction for four counts of fraud for deceiving investors.

Because Fielder couldn’t record his conversations with Holmes following her imprisonment, he recruited Amanda Seyfried to recreate those encounters. Seyfried previously played Holmes in the 2022 biopic The Dropout .

Seyfried’s involvement in You Can See Everything was initially kept under wraps. But, with the documentary now available to stream in the US , she’s started doing interviews about her involvement in the project which could see her become the first documentary star to win an acting Oscar.

“At first, it was never my intention to recreate Elizabeth Holmes ever again,” Seyfried said during an appearance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon . Fielder originally reached out to “pick her brains” about her role in The Dropout after Emma Stone connected them. “We talked for an hour on Facetime, he told me he had lived with her for a month before she went to prison. I didn’t expect it.”

Fielder asked her a “bunch of questions” before offering her the chance to see the footage they’d shot for the documentary, if they could film her reaction. Eventually Seyfried started playing the part of Holmes.

items.t: Amanda Seyfried had to get a five-factor security app just to read ‘You Can See Everything’ script

items.title: Travis Barker Says Phil Collins Suggested They ‘Do Something Together’ Following Rock Hall Induction Ceremony
items.summary:
Phil Collins has called time on touring, but he’s not against a collaboration with blink-182’s Travis Barker .

That was one of the unlikely outcomes of the Rock And Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony last weekend, at which Barker had the honors of saluting fellow drummer Collins.

Barker stopped by ABC’s Jimmy Kimmel Live on Tuesday night (Nov. 24), for a chat about his growing tapestry of tattoos (he does get approval from his wife, Kourtney Kardashian, if they’re above his shoulders), his documentary, and the career highlight that was his moment at the podium, with Collins by his side — thanks to a rare mistimed moment from the veteran British rocker.

“I was a huge Phil Collins fan. My mom introduced me to him when I was really young. Four, five, six years old,” Barker tells Kimmel. The youngster studied Collins’ work behind the kit, listened to his tunes until the grooves in the records wore out.

Barker overcame some obstacles on the way to giving Collins his dues. He was “sick as a dog all week,” and speeches, he doesn’t do them. “This is all new for me, but he’s such a big inspiration to me.” It was Barker’s 51st birthday too. He wasn’t missing that present.

Following the speech, Barker returned to his comfort zone — behind the drumkit — for a performance of “In The Air Tonight” with Cynthia Erivo on vocals.

After the spot, he got a heathy pair of thumbs-up from Collins and emails were later shared. “He was like ‘I loved your performance. It meant so much to me and we should do something together,’” he remarked. Perhaps a Genesis update. We’ll wait and see.…
items.t: Travis Barker Says Phil Collins Suggested They ‘Do Something Together’ Following Rock Hall Induction Ceremony

items.title: AI music banned on TIDAL as they delete 29million songs
items.summary:
AI music has been banned on TIDAL, and the platform has taken down nearly 30 million songs identified as being “100 per cent AI generated recordings”.

READ MORE: What does the music industry want from the future of AI – and how can the UK lead the way? 

The change comes as the use of AI in music has become increasingly prominent in recent years, and a study conducted last year revealed that 97 per cent of people “can’t tell the difference” between real and AI music .

In June, TIDAL confirmed that it was putting a new policy in place to crack down on AI-generated music – revealing that it would no longer be paying royalties to any music made entirely by artificial intelligence.

The guidelines clarified that “artists should have the freedom to create with AI tools”, and would only be affecting music that is made entirely by “text-prompted AI”. It also said that while AI could exist on the platform, it would be offering people the option to filter it out as “listeners should have the autonomy to choose the type of content they consume”.

Now, the platform has revealed that it will be banning AI music entirely from next month.

“Since July, we’ve demonetised and labeled 100 per cent AI generated recordings. Now, we’re banning these tracks from TIDAL entirely,” a new post on TIDAL’s social media read. “If a distributor tells us a track was created solely using generative AI tools, or if we detect that it was, we’ll remove it from TIDAL.”

View this post on Instagram 

The post also shared some statistics, confirming that just 6 per cent of its “entire streaming catalogue…
items.t: AI music banned on TIDAL as they delete 29million songs

items.title: Phoebe Bridgers live in Dublin: singer-songwriter is on another planet
items.summary:
In the lead-up to the release of Phoebe Bridgers ’ third album, ‘Lost Weekend’ , the musician turned to an old promo idea from the ’70s and ’80s: giving fans a first listen at planetariums worldwide. The idea has carried over into the corresponding Lost Tour, too: NME enters Dublin’s 3Arena on night two of her UK/Europe tour (November 24) to see a stage turned into a mobile planetarium, complete with projections, lasers, lights and dry ice.

READ MORE: Phoebe Bridgers – ‘Lost Weekend’ review: indie’s poet laureate returns with a staggering, strange and stirring opus 

A giant white dome takes over the entirety of the main stage – so much so that support act Isaac Wood + Anaïs warm up the crowd from the circular b-stage at the back of the room (Wood making an anticipated return to music after leaving Black Country, New Road in 2022). Once it’s time for Bridgers to begin, a cratered black orb glows green, floating up and down as the light intensifies, the singer-songwriter’s disembodied voice delivering a spectral version of ‘The Outside’. It’s spooky and spacey – half feeling like aliens are about to enter the equation, and half like we’ve been flung into deep space. As the opening chords of ‘Motion Sickness’ thunder across the room, the dome lifts up to reveal Bridgers and her nine-piece band (including “the leader” Jay Som ) ready to take us on a journey out of this world.

items.title: Shouting from the margins, Bricknasty give a voice to Dublin’s sidelined youth
items.summary:
A swell of Gen Z Dubliners linger by the doorway of hip city centre clothing store Emporium. Excited grins and sickly-sweet vapes abound, as inside Bricknasty – one of the Irish capital’s most innovative, sonically distinctive young acts – launch their new EP ‘Forever’ with a packed-out playback event. They didn’t expect this kind of crowd. “We’re gonna swap who’s inside and outside because it’s not fair. This is fucked up!” shouts charismatic frontman Fatboy, perched on the windowsill in a bright green Ireland bobble hat and black jacket.

The five-piece Bricknasty was originally formed by Fatboy and producer Cillian McCauley during the COVID-19 pandemic, after the pair connected online. “It was just horrible pictures being sent back and forth”, McCauley jokes when NME sits down with him, Fatboy (Jonathan Ambrose) and bassist Chris LaMotte earlier in the day. “I was a simple country boy from County Cavan when our paths collided; I quickly became something much different.”

After completing their line-up by recruiting drummer Korey Thomas, and former bassist Dara Abdurahman and saxophonist/keys player Louis Younge, Bricknasty kicked off an intriguing pattern: four releases in four years (culminating with ‘Forever’), each time following extremely intense, soul-searching, socially conscious projects with breezier EPs that allow them to blow off some steam. “I think we’re finished with that cycle now,” reflects Fatboy. “But we look at those four EPs like a college course: we wanted to experience as much of music as possible.”

Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach shimmied off with the Len Goodman Mirrorball trophy after winning season 35 of ABC’s Dancing With The Stars .

In doing so, Frech, the two-time Paralympic gold medalist for Team U.S.A. in track and field, becomes the first amputee winner of the celebrity dance-off.

The finale episode on Tuesday night (Nov. 24) saw contestants compete in three rounds. And finally, each couple contested the freestyle round — the make-or-break business end of the popular show.

The winning pair hit a freestyle soundtracked by Linkin Park’s “Numb.” Ezra began the number without his prosthetic on, and had a problem with it slipping during the routine. They recovered, and the judges loved it. Carrie Ann Inaba, Derek Hough and Bruno Tonioli awarded 30/30.

items.title: ‘A True Giant of the Music Industry’: King Charles Remembers Ian ‘Molly’ Meldrum And Their Infamous Interview
items.summary:
In showbiz, W.C. Fields is famously quoted as saying, never work with kids or animals. For Ian “Molly” Meldrum, the late Australian broadcaster and record producer might’ve done well to avoid working with the future King of England.

Molly, as he’s known to millions, gave a gift that continues to give when he interviewed the-then Prince Charles on Countdown back in 1977. The subject was a fine one, albeit a switch-up from the regular kings of rock and pop who dropped by — some of whom weren’t on their best behavior for national TV .

On that occasion, it was the host who bombed. Molly, despite conducting countless interviews for the camera, fumbled and sweated through the interview, so obviously star-stuck by his famous royal guest. 

It was television gold. 

When news of Molly’s death reached Buckingham Palace, King Charles paid tribute to the late music legend and remembered the unforgettable exchange.

An aide to the King said he had been “deeply saddened” to hear of Meldrum’s death, the BBC reports .

“His Majesty’s interview with Molly is a moment he and many others will never forget – he hopes that interview will once again raise a few smiles as Australians honor Molly’s legacy as a true giant of the music industry.”

Molly, the late ex- Countdown host and music industry veteran, died on Monday after a long illness, at the age of 83.

Elton John is one of many international stars of the music community who has remembered Molly as both “an Australian legend and an institution.”

Fellow Rock And Roll Hall of Fame inductees Duran Duran reflect on Molly as a loveable…

items.title: Matthew Capper, Late Music Publishing Exec, Honored With New Award
items.summary:
SYDNEY, Australia — Matthew Capper is saluted with a new, annual award which bears his name.

Announced Wednesday, Nov. 25, the Matthew Capper Award recognizes integrity, generosity, professionalism, commitment and service to music publishing in Australia and New Zealand, and is presented by the Australasian Music Publishers’ Association Limited (AMPAL).

Capper, the long-time former Warner Chappell Australia managing director and AMPAL chair, died unexpectedly in January 2025 following a surgical procedure. He was 47, just one month shy of his 48th birthday.

“Matthew was widely respected for his integrity, professionalism, intelligence, humor, generosity and unwavering commitment to creators and the music publishing community,” reads a statement from AMPAL, announcing the new honor.

“A passionate advocate for music publishing, Matthew believed in the importance of doing things properly, ethically and in service of the broader industry. His approach to professional life reflected a belief that lasting contributions are measured not simply by individual achievements, but by the positive difference we make to those around us.”

In 2005, Capper became the youngest person ever appointed to the AMCOS board at the age of just 28. Two years later, in 2007, he became the youngest to join the APRA board, at 30.

He went on to serve as AMPAL chair for 11 years, as a non-executive director of APRA and AMCOS for more than 16 years, and as GM and managing director of Warner Chappell for over 20 years. On the international front, he served as a non-executive director and treasurer of…
items.t: Matthew Capper, Late Music Publishing Exec, Honored With New Award

The Dolly Parton estate has announced the leadership of its creative team led by Steve Summers , who worked with Parton for more than 30 years and will serve as the estate’s creative director.

Summers will steer a team that also includes creative manager Riley Reed Hanratty , design specialist Vance Nichols and creative specialist Bradley Schnabel . Framed is one of the newest, following in the footsteps of Wordle , but offering a slightly different twist. You’ll still need to work out the answer using limited information and only six tries, but it’ll be movies that you’ll be guessing.

You see, Framed focuses on individual frames, or stills, of an ever-changing roster of movies. Some show a fair amount of action at the start, while others will take careful analysis and decent trivia knowledge to crack. With each wrong guess, a new still is revealed, hopefully adding enough extra information and context for you to guess the correct movie title.

With only six guesses at your disposal, you may need a little help guessing today’s Framed answer. To give you a hint, we’ve included some clues that will tease the title of the movie picked as today’s puzzle. The date in the capital will cap off the band’s UK tour victory lap for acclaimed fourth album ‘Forever’. The honour of stepping onto the hallowed Brixton Academy stage was not lost on them.

“I can’t believe we are playing there,” singer Jules Jackson told NME . “I have so so so many happy memories of being at shows in that building since I was a teenager. I’m pinching myself. I can’t wait to yell along to our songs with everyone.”

Have they any surprises up their sleeves for the show?

“We have a load of new stage props which weve never had before,” Jackson replied. “So the show is going to be slick as hell. I’m hoping for high drama. It’s been so fun planning it out. Also some incredible lights which we are hoping will transport us into the galaxy.”

The Big Moon, 2026. Credit: Melanie Lehmann

items.title: ‘My name was poison’: Donny Osmond on fame, failure – and his friend Michael Jackson
items.summary:
He was the child star of the Osmonds who become a global celebrity by 14. Then, at 21, his career came crashing down. Here, he reveals how he survived his years in exile – and what happened when Jackson was accused of child abuse

For a brief period in the early 1970s, Donny Osmond ruled the world. He was the global teenage heart-throb. Even Michael Jackson trailed behind him. He was 14 when his most famous song, Puppy Love, spent five weeks at No 1 in the UK. My sister had a huge poster of him on her bedroom wall. Then again, everybody’s sister had a poster of him on their bedroom wall. Between 1972 and 1973 he had six Top 5 hits in the UK, three of them No 1s (including The Twelfth of Never and Young Love). He was equally successful back home in the US.

Osmond was clean-cut, religious and respectful, with a mighty ability to punch out cover versions of saccharine standards. From his purple velvet cap to his doleful eyes and dazzling all-American smile, he was a marketing dream. We’d only just finished with Beatlemania. And now there was Donnymania.

items.t: ‘My name was poison’: Donny Osmond on fame, failure – and his friend Michael Jackson

items.title: Interpol and Bloc Party review – two of 00s indie’s most revered acts go toe-to-toe
items.summary:
Utilita Arena Cardiff
Kele Okereke has a tough challenge selling Bloc Party’s trite latest album – a far cry from Interpol’s ‘masterpiece’ eighth record, performed here to darkly hypnotic effect

Try as one might to resist comparison, the balance of this particular yin and yang has been shifting for some time. Twelve months ago, when Interpol and Bloc Party announced a UK and European co-headline tour, the pairing looked like an even contest: two of 00s indie’s most revered acts, whose landmark debuts remain touchstones of the era.

Since then, their fortunes have diverged. As an opening bass drone strafes the room, Bloc Party arrive in Cardiff in superficially fine, if puzzling, form. Their seventh album, Anatomy of a Brief Romance, has been met with diminishing returns, its Snapchat-caption triteness – “Every day is such a vibe”, runs one refrain – and creative inertia doing little to win over listeners.

items.title: Fontaines DC review – thrilling gothic grandeur from a band vaulting into greatness
items.summary:
M&S Bank Arena, Liverpool
Just a few years since playing little dive bars, the Irish rockers have confidently scaled up to huge rooms like this – and are now one of the key interpreters of modern malaise

A mere seven years since their debut, Dogrel, Fontaines DC have enjoyed a virtually seamless passage from Dublin dive bars to arenas, with stadiums to follow next year. Each step has been taken seemingly effortlessly in their stride and this latest outing is no exception. Bathed in shimmering blue light, the band are well into hymnal opener Six Shot Morning before we even see sight of singer Grian Chatten. He wanders on while singing, an entrance worthy of Frank Sinatra.

Chatten has previously seemed to distrust showbiz, but if anything the singer seems far more comfortable on the bigger stage than he ever did on smaller ones. With his Korn T-shirt, unfeasibly baggy trousers and tiny tattoo reading “deadly” in capitals, he leaps around, raises his arms to whip up the crowd and points the microphone towards them to sing key lines. Similarly, music this intense, dark, elegiac and even bleak – which speaks to the void at the heart of much modern life – is hardly typical arena fare but works brilliantly by taking on a more anthemic, celebratory aspect. It’s certainly weirdly thrilling hearing Chatten’s lines such as “We’re all depressed, running on a wheel” or “I don’t feel anything in the modern world” – or a song as plainly dark as Jackie Down the Line – become enormous, arena-uniting sing-songs.
items.t: Fontaines DC review – thrilling gothic grandeur from a band vaulting into greatness

items.title: The week’s best new tracks and the act you need to know: the rangy folk-prog songwriting of Threshold
items.summary:
Isaac Eiger’s solo venture leaves jangle pop behind for a wilder sound. Often it owes a debt to Alex G, but what indie-rock song doesn’t these days?

From New York via Montana
Recommended if you like Cameron Winter, Tobias Jesso Jr, Alex G
Up next Supporting Caroline on tour in Canada and the US until 19 November

Isaac Eiger is something of a scene legend in the world of American indie-rock. Raised in Bozeman, Montana, he was the founder and lead singer of the cult shoegaze-adjacent six-piece Strange Ranger, who left heartbroken a small, fervent fanbase when they announced their breakup in 2023. Taking a discernibly British approach to their sound, Strange Ranger traversed C86-y jangle-pop before landing on Madchester rave-up for their final album, 2023’s Pure Music. But Eiger is nothing if not musically worldly: he has written and produced with both underground heroes (Cassandra Jenkins, Chanel Beads) and nascent pop stars (Adéla, Frost Children).

Ever-prolific, Eiger also has a solo project under the name Threshold, with which he released a gauzy, 19-minute EP in 2024 called Thief. Earlier this year, he released Stillwater, the first single from the debut Threshold album, due for release in 2027 on the London-based label Untitled.
